claim: Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020) report regret of order sqrt(T) when the horizon T and the initial resources are scaled proportionally, and an Omega(sqrt T) lower bound for any algorithm, so that order is optimal; the Theorem 1 bound itself holds for any T >= 1, with constants in the bounds on revenue and consumption, and only the optimality of the order is asymptotic (txt 74-79, 370-372).
Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020) state that their algorithms never deplete resources too early: with probability 1 the stopping time is within a constant of T (Proposition 2).
note: The constant is about the multiplier cap over the step size; the authors call the result new in the allocation literature.

claim: Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020) target a constant resource use per period so resources run out exactly at the end of the horizon, raising the dual variable when a request uses more than the target and lowering it when less (txt 99-106).
Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020): the constant in the regret bound depends on the number of resources m, and the authors call that dependence sub-optimal (txt 380-390).
Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020) report no measured gain for budget bidding; their only numerical experiment is on proportional matching and 'verifies the results in Theorem 1' (txt 576-584).
Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020) give the bidding form w_t = v_t/(1 + mu_t): bid the value shrunk by one plus the dual price (txt 505-516).
note: Symbol mu_t is lost in the text extraction; the form is as quoted in the collect file.

claim: Balseiro, Lu and Mirrokni (2020) assume a horizon T known in advance, requests i.i.d. from an unknown finite-support distribution, and resources that cannot be replenished once consumed (txt ~334-352, ~346).
note: The text line numbers are approximate in the collect file.

claim: Gaitonde, Li, Light, Lucier and Slivkins (2023): the agent lowers its multiplier when the target rate is above the current expenditure and raises it when below, by an amount proportional to the deviation (txt 243).

Gaitonde et al. (2023): Algorithm 1 does not run out of budget too early, a property proved in Lemma 2.2 of Balseiro and Gur; it needs a multiplier cap at least v_max/rho - 1, a step with eps*v_max <= 1 and a payment never above the bid, and the guarantee is a gap of at most mu_bar/(eps rho) + v_max/rho rounds, a fixed number of rounds that can be a large share of a short horizon (txt 246-258, 262-300).
note: Narrowed per refuter a1-refute-1 A05; the gap formula is garbled in the text and read as the refuter reads it.

claim: Gaitonde et al. (2023) obtain regret O(T^(3/4)) against the best fixed multiplier in hindsight, with the i.i.d.-opponents case and a step size that does not need to know the drift (txt 37).
note: The O(T^(3/4)) bound is the dynamic-environment rate; the sqrt(T) rate is in the next record.

claim: Gaitonde et al. (2023) note that Algorithm 1 is known to achieve a sqrt(T) regret rate in this setting, citing their references 13 and 17 (txt 1230).
Gaitonde et al. (2023) report that, without convergence, the aggregate outcome reaches at least half of the optimal expected liquid welfare (txt 27, 7).

Gaitonde et al. (2023): in adversarial environments budgeted bidding admits no regret bound against a time-invariant benchmark, only approximation ratios, because of the spend-or-save dilemma; against the weaker perfect-pacing-sequence benchmark the paper proves vanishing regret for gradient pacing, with a bound that grows with the total change of the perfect multipliers (txt 101, 108, 115).
note: Narrowed per refuter a1-refute-1 A06.

claim: Gaitonde et al. (2023), in a semi-synthetic simulation on Bing Advertising data, report a regret rate less than T^(3/5) against the best fixed multiplier in hindsight (txt 102).
note: A simulation on logged data, not a live system; the text read gives no percent gain.

claim: Gaitonde et al. (2023), same Bing simulation: Adam has an improved regret rate at the expense of lower aggregate liquid welfare, MU is dominated by their Algorithm 1, and OGD performs comparably (txt 102-103).
note: Simulation, as in the previous record.

claim: Chen et al. (2022): in the stochastic case pacing is generally superior to throttling for the advertiser, in line with pacing being asymptotically optimal there (txt 18).
note: Theory only; no experiment in the part read.

claim: Chen et al. (2022): any throttling strategy has an Omega(sqrt T) expected regret lower bound with stochastic values (txt 33, 238), and their OGD-CB reaches O(sqrt(T) log T) (txt 71, 266).
Chen et al. (2022): with adversarial values no throttling strategy's asymptotic competitive ratio can exceed the average budget divided by the maximum value (Theorem 3.2, txt 33, 247).
Chen et al. (2022): if the competing price is adversarial, any throttling strategy can behave arbitrarily badly (Theorem 3.3, txt 33).

Conitzer et al. (2018), in a static pacing-game model: with one multiplier per buyer, the best multiplier makes the budget run out exactly at the end of the period, unless the buyer would not run out even at multiplier 1 (txt 28).
note: Static model; narrowed per refuter a1-refute-1 A10.

claim: Conitzer et al. (2018): probabilistic throttling runs the budget out around the end of the period but misses opportunities where the buyer could have won at lower cost (txt 27).

Conitzer et al. (2018) give, as a stated reason for the wide use of multiplicative pacing, that it lets a buyer participate in more auctions and win at lower prices than probabilistic throttling, backed by a citation to Balseiro et al. (2021), who find it buyer-optimal among the options they study; it is not a result shown in this paper (txt 28-29).
note: Narrowed per refuter a1-refute-1 A10. The cited Balseiro et al. (2021) source was not opened.

claim: Conitzer et al. (2018) state that in practice equilibrium multiplicity is rarely an issue (txt ~34).
note: The text line is approximate in the collect file.

claim: Conitzer et al. (2018), from the abstract: a market can have multiple pacing equilibria with large variations in several natural objectives.
note: Read as a summary of the abstract, not quoted.

claim: Conitzer et al. (2018), worked example and not a measurement: shading a bid from the value to $2 gives 7 wins and utility $25, against 6 wins and utility $20 on a $10 budget, a 25 percent utility gain (txt 25).
note: Illustration from a figure note; not a production measurement.

claim: Xu, Lee, Li, Qi and Lu (Yahoo, 2015, self-reported) re-plan the remaining budget over the remaining slots so that the planned slot spends sum to the remaining budget B_m (txt 196-207).

Xu et al. (2015, Yahoo, self-reported) give three reasons for choosing probabilistic throttling over bid modification: the bid win-rate curve is usually not smooth and the bid landscape shifts, so modifying the bid can cause significant changes in spend; reserve prices can block a lowered bid; and a throttling rate decouples pacing control from bid calculation (txt 133).
note: Narrowed per refuter a1-refute-1 A13 (the earlier text gave the first reason only).

claim: Xu et al. (2015, Yahoo, self-reported) rejected a single global pacing threshold, since ad requests are not smoothly distributed over response rate, making smooth control with one threshold difficult (txt 440).
Xu et al. (2015, Yahoo, self-reported): against a one-rate baseline on three real campaigns over 24 hours, eCPC changed by -72%, -67% and -79% (txt 446).
note: The paper credits the gain to better impression choice, not to the pacing loop.

claim: Xu et al. (2015, Yahoo, self-reported): spend smoothness is unchanged against the one-rate baseline, AvgErr 6.4% against 6.8%, 9.1% against 9.2% and 10.2% against 9.8% on the three campaigns (txt 446), baseline first.

Xu et al. (2015, Yahoo, self-reported), over-time test on four campaigns (baseline in week one, method in week two): eCPC cut by up to almost -50% and spend within a 13.9% deviation from the spending plan (txt 447).

Xu et al. (2015, Yahoo, self-reported), in an offline simulation of one campaign with 1-minute slots and 10,000,000 requests against the controller of Agarwal et al. (LinkedIn): AvgErr 96 percent for the Agarwal et al. controller against 18 percent for their own method (txt 672).
note: Corrected: the 96 percent is the Agarwal et al. controller's figure and the 18 percent is the paper's own; checked at paper text line 672.

claim: Xu et al. (2015) assume very many requests per slot, tens of billions a day on the platform (txt 61).

Agarwal, Ghosh, Wei and You (LinkedIn, 2014, self-reported) multiply the pass-through rate by 1 + r or 1 - r each window, with a constant r of 10 percent and a slow start at 10 percent (txt 58-59, 73, 75).
note: Read from a university reading-list copy of the full paper; figures as extracted, not checked against the ACM original.

claim: Agarwal et al. (2014, LinkedIn, self-reported): a textbook spend-to-budget throttle gave 'an improvement in revenue but not a significant increase in campaign life' (txt 64).
note: Read from a university reading-list copy of the full paper.

claim: Agarwal et al. (2014, LinkedIn, self-reported): the daily plan assumes no traffic in the last two hours, so budget is meant to be gone in 22 hours, a fast finish (txt 78).
note: Read from a university reading-list copy of the full paper.

claim: Agarwal, Ghosh, Wei and You (LinkedIn, 2014, self-reported), Direct Ads, alternate days over 2 weeks: median campaign life (time to spend 95 percent of the budget) rose from 13.54 h with pacing off to 19.50 h on, an increase of 44 percent (txt table 2, 150).
note: Direct Ads means demand exceeds supply. Narrowed per refuter a1-refute-1 A16 (95 percent definition). Figures from a university reading-list copy; table values as extracted.

claim: Agarwal et al. (2014, LinkedIn, self-reported), Direct Ads, pacing on against off: unique impressions per spend +7.74% and cost per request +5.67% (txt table 2).
note: Table values as extracted from the reading-list copy.

claim: Agarwal, Ghosh, Wei and You (LinkedIn, 2014, self-reported), Sponsored Status Updates where supply exceeds demand: median campaign life (time to spend 95 percent of the budget) rose from 6.92 h off to 17.25 h on, a gain the paper gives as 149 percent (txt table 3, 264-265).
note: Narrowed per refuter a1-refute-1 A16 (95 percent definition). Table values as extracted from the reading-list copy.

claim: Agarwal et al. (2014, LinkedIn, self-reported), Sponsored Status Updates: unique impressions per spend +10.52%, cost per request +0.96%, and over-delivery from 4.12% to 2.39%, which the paper gives as 42 percent less (txt table 3).
note: Table values as extracted from the reading-list copy.

claim: Agarwal et al. (2014) assume a daily plan fixed at the start of the day from a traffic forecast, and spend information that arrives with a delay (txt 33, 154).
